newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Indonesian oil product thirst to last into April.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian oil product thirst to last into April.

text.p: Indonesia's thirst for diesel, jet-kerosene fuel and gasoline during the first quarter is not expected to be quenched until after April due to high seasonal demand and refinery problems, industry sources said on Thursday.

"The high demand is due to the recent festive season such as Christmas, New Year and Hari Raya," a source with national oil firm Pertamina said. "The requirements for the Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca) season are still being awaited."
The Moslem Eid-ul Adha celebrations marking the feast of sacrifice, which is the climax of the Hajj, falls on April 18 but pilgrims normally travel to Saudi Arabia more than a month ahead.

Indonesia, which is 90 percent Moslem, normally imports higher volumes of jet fuel during the Hajj season. Traders said they would buy at least the same volume in April as in February and March -- between 1.3 million and 1.5 million barrels.
Some traders said Indonesia might have bought even more than 1.5 million barrels in March.
Indonesia normally imports less than one million barrels of jet fuel a month.

Traders said the recent rally in jet fuel prices was largely due to sellers pricing out their sales into Indonesia. Over the past week, jet prices have surged by $2.00 per barrel to last trade on Wednesday at $29.50.
Indonesia bought around five million barrels of diesel a month in November and December and continued big purchases into February and March at around 4.0 million barrels a month, traders said.
They are expected to take as much in April. The country's usual monthly purchases are around 3.0 million barrels.

Indonesia's gasoline demand also jumped recently to about 500,000 barrels for March deliveries to cover shortages resulting from technical problems at the Balongan refinery as well as the current shutdown at the Dumai refinery.
Traders said most of the gasoline requirements had been covered. Indonesia's monthly imports normally do not exceed 200,000 barrels.
The 120,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) Dumai facility in Sumatra was shut for a 38-day maintenance on February 22.
The 125,000-bpd Balongan plant has been shut intermittently since February 6, which also contributed to disruption in oil product supplies.

Traders said whether Indonesia continued to buy more than normal monthly volumes of oil products beyond April would depend largely on how soon the problems at Balongan could be overcome and when the Dumai refinery would actually restart.
